views.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Respond to the imminent US$200bn List 3 tariffs with calibrated, proportionate retaliation while keeping the negotiating channel open and avoiding a maximum-escalation spiral. Do not capitulate on Made in China 2025, but also do not mirror Trump's escalation dollar-for-dollar into a full US$500bn tariff war, since we lack symmetric import capacity and a widening war hurts our export economy and FX stability more than it hurts them.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is high and rising. The US has already imposed 25% tariffs on US$50bn of our goods (List 1 on July 6 and List 2 on Aug 23, both matched by our retaliation), and the public-comment period on the additional US$200bn at 10%—with the administration publicly weighing raising it to 25% (timeline Aug 1)—expires exactly at our decision date, with tariffs likely unveiled immediately after. Talks in Washington on Aug 22-23 ended with no follow-on scheduled, and our own officials signaled we may wait for the November US midterms. This directly targets our export economy (US-bound goods run ~US$500bn/year) and, more seriously, the demand to roll back Made in China 2025 strikes at our core tech-autonomy goals; the earlier ZTE denial order showed firm-level vulnerability. Macro/currency evidence reinforces the strain: the renminbi has depreciated ~7% since April under PBOC-managed drift, raising capital-flight and reserves concerns, and analysts warn a sharp devaluation would be too costly. Yet the situation is not existential: we hold large FX reserves, a sizable trade surplus, and the yuan slide partially cushions the tariff hit. Given the asymmetry (we import far less than we export), maximal escalation is self-defeating and would invite Trump's stated additional-US$200bn response; a measured, proportional retaliation preserves our negotiating credibility and domestic legitimacy without provoking the full spiral. Hence a mild-escalation stance (retaliate) rather than either capitulation or all-out war, justified by the genuinely high but buffer-mitigated threat.
key_factors: US$200bn List 3 (10%, possibly rising to 25%) imminent as comment period closes Sept 6
US$50bn in tariffs already in effect, matched by China's retaliation
Demand to roll back Made in China 2025 targets core tech-autonomy/CCP legitimacy
Yuan down ~7% since April; FX/capital-flight and reserves pressure
Aug 22-23 talks ended with no progress and no follow-on scheduled
Asymmetric trade: China imports far less from US, limiting retaliation capacity

sources_cited.excerpt: List 2 tariffs take effect: US 25% on ~$16B (completing the $50B package). China imposes matching ~$16B retaliation.
USTR says it is considering raising the proposed List 3 rate from 10% to 25%.
US Commerce Department bans ZTE from buying US components (denial order).
US and China were negotiating in Washington... a senior admin official... talks have gone nowhere; USTR moving forward with $200bn in tariffs.
Yuan has already lost 7% against the US dollar in the last four months as trade tensions rise; exports to the US account for roughly a fifth of total shipments.
Renminbi has fallen over 7 percent... China exports far more to the US than it imports, so it cannot respond with tariffs on anywhere near the same amount.
Analysts say yuan depreciation as a tool in a trade war would be too costly... could tip balance of payments into a notable deficit.
